title: Gender Differences in Tackling Fake News: Different Degrees of Concern, but Same Problems
screen_reason: The paper's aim is gender differences in concern about and detection of fake news (both ineligible), but Tables 5 and 6 report the share of a representative Spanish survey sample (N = 998/1,001) who say they receive fake news on each topic, e.g. 65.1% naming politics among the three topics of fake news they most frequently receive. That is a self-reported receipt share with a stated denominator, so RECALL. Concern (mean 6.12/7) and self-assessed detection difficulty (67.13%) are NOT extracted.

estimates.platform: not specified (general question about fake news received)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who name politics among the (up to three) topics on which they believe they most frequently receive fake news
estimates.denominator: 998 respondents to the topic question, from a stratified representative online survey of 1,001 Spaniards aged 18+ (Gesop)
estimates.definition: Respondent cited 'politics' among up to three topics when asked which topics of fake news they most frequently receive
estimates.misinfo_def: "for ordinary people, fake news is the most popular and frequently used expression to refer to the nebula of false information, viral lies, conspiracy theories, and other forms of misleading information spread on social networks and some news media (in Spanish, noticias falsas)" [English translation of the Spanish term: 'false news']

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement; no external verification of any received item. Multi-answer question, up to three topics; 20.8% answered DK/NO.
estimates.moderator_quote: Respondents were asked to cite up to three topics on which they believe they receive fake news most frequently (Table 6).
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATION FLAG. The question presupposes receipt: it asks which topics of fake news you receive, not whether you receive any, so this is a topic-conditional receipt share rather than a clean overall recall rate. The paper never reports the share receiving fake news on ANY topic; the only route to it would be 100 - 20.8 (DK/NO), a complement R8 forbids. breadth coded 'false' from the Spanish term 'noticias falsas' used with respondents, though the authors' gloss stretches to 'other forms of misleading information'.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted, ineligible: concern about the spread of fake news (mean 6.12 on 1-7; Table 2 gives the full distribution, 26.87% answering 6 and 52.55% answering 7) - this is an attitude, not a perceived amount of misinformation, and the 'worried' share (6 or 7) would require summing two categories, which R8 forbids. 2) NOT extracted, ineligible: '67.13% admit to having difficulties in detecting fake news', '76.8% of concerned citizens report having difficulty in detecting fake news', '63.58% among the least worried' - self-assessed discernment, explicitly excluded. 3) Other topic shares in Table 6 are verbatim and could each be a row on the same measure with a different topic code: immigration 38.4%, nationalism 36.9%, society/crime 32.5%, feminism 28.4%, celebrities 25.8%, science/tech 7.1%, sports 6.4%, DK/NO 20.8%. Only the politics rows were extracted (the paper's headline topic and the only one the review's topic codes handle cleanly); an adjudicator may want the rest. 4) Gender-split values (nationalism 42.0% men vs 31.8% women; celebrities 29.4% women vs 22.1% men; sport 9.4% vs 3.4%) are the paper's headline contrast but are demographic subgroup splits of the same measure, so not extracted. 5) No overall 'received any fake news' share exists anywhere in the paper. 6) Table 4 (factors used to assess trustworthiness: source 64.53%, sharer 52.20%, etc.) and the verification-frequency figures (42% of the concerned check frequently vs 32.7% of the less concerned) are behavioural responses to fake news, not exposure.

rob.design: Online questionnaire administered by the market research firm Gesop to a national sample of N = 1,001 Spaniards aged 18+, stratified by age, sex and autonomous community against the actual population distribution; sampling error +/- 3.2 at 95% confidence; fieldwork 24-30 April 2019. Tables 5 and 6 have N = 998. No response rate, no panel provider details and no incentive information reported. All measures are single self-report items; no content was collected or coded, so there is no ground truth, no coding procedure and no reliability statistic. The key item presupposes receipt of fake news (it asks which topics, not whether), and the term used with respondents was the colloquial 'noticias falsas' ('false news'), which the authors themselves note is interpreted more loosely by the public than by researchers. Analysis by t-tests, chi-square and proportion comparisons at p = .05. Partially funded by WhatsApp Inc.; authors state the funder had no role.
rob.item6_quote: for ordinary people, fake news is the most popular and frequently used expression to refer to the nebula of false information, viral lies, conspiracy theories, and other forms of misleading information spread on social networks and some news media (in Spanish, noticias falsas). Since the research is based on a survey of a representative sample of the Spanish population, we decided to use the most familiar word in order to avoid misunderstanding.
rob.item10_quote: Respondents were asked to cite up to three topics on which they believe they receive fake news most frequently (Table 6). When analyzing the three responses, politics remains the main topic, although does not show any differences between genders.
